title: The Conservatory Recital
scenes: Scene 1. Leonhard Askew, sixty-four, taught piano at the Vesterbro conservatory for twenty-two years and was found dead at the keyboard of practice room 4 on the evening of the winter recital, slumped forward, the door locked from inside with the old brass key still in it. The caretaker Jonas Pirk forced the door at seven when the recital was due to start. The room has one window, painted shut years ago. The first assumption is a heart attack; Askew had a known condition and took digitalis for it.

Scene 2. Inspector Halloran takes the names of everyone in the building between five and seven. Vera Askew, the wife, who had come to hear the recital and sat in the hall from half past five. Dmitri Sorel, a former student turned rival teacher, who had argued with Askew that afternoon about a pupil who switched to him. Agnes Holm, the conservatory's secretary, who manages the keys and the schedules. Felix Brand, Askew's star pupil, who was to play the recital's last piece. Ruth Kessler, the accompanist, who had rehearsed with Askew's pupils all week. Jonas Pirk, the caretaker.

Scene 3. Agnes Holm explains the keys. Each practice room has one brass key, kept on a board in her office when not in use; room 4 was signed out to Askew at four and never signed back. There is a master key in a locked drawer of her desk, and she alone has the drawer key, which she wears on a ribbon. Halloran checks the drawer: the master is there, and Agnes says she has not opened the drawer since Monday.

Scene 4. Dmitri Sorel makes no secret of his feelings. Askew, he says, had been poaching his best pupil, Felix Brand, for years, and that afternoon told him in front of two students that Sorel 'teaches the fingers and not the music'. Sorel left the building at half past five, he says, and walked by the canal to cool off; nobody saw him until he reappeared for the recital at a quarter to seven.

Scene 5. The doctor's first report: death between half past five and half past six, consistent with cardiac arrest. There is a half-finished cup of coffee on the piano lid, cold, and a glass of water with the dregs of something white at the bottom. Askew's digitalis was in his jacket, the bottle three-quarters full. The doctor takes the glass away without comment.

Scene 6. Felix Brand, nineteen, is distraught and cannot be questioned for long. He says he last saw his teacher at a quarter past five, when Askew sent him to warm up in room 2 and said he wanted 'half an hour alone with the Schubert'. Felix says Askew seemed well, a little tired, and asked Felix to bring him a coffee from the staff room, which Felix did, leaving it on the lid at about twenty past five.

Scene 7. Ruth Kessler is calm and useful. She had rehearsed with Felix and two others that week and knows the building well. She says she spent the hour before the recital in the hall, tuning the second piano with Jonas Pirk, which Pirk confirms: they were together from five until the doors opened at half past six, except for ten minutes when she went to fetch sheet music from the library on the second floor.

Scene 8. Vera Askew says her husband had been 'impossible' for a month: sleeping badly, forgetting lessons, convinced that someone at the conservatory was 'going through his things'. She mentions, as if it hardly matters, that she is twenty years younger than him and that the marriage was 'a working arrangement'. She has a lover, Halloran learns later from the caretaker, who is not among the people in the building.

Scene 9. Jonas Pirk describes forcing the door. The key was in the lock on the inside, turned; he had to split the frame. He adds that the window has been painted shut since the roof repairs in 2019, and that room 4 is the only practice room whose key sticks, 'you have to lift it and turn, everyone who uses that room knows the trick'. Halloran tries it: lifted and turned, the key works smoothly from either side with the door closed, if you have a second key.

Scene 10. The library on the second floor keeps a sign-out book. Ruth Kessler's name is there at 5:48 for 'Brahms op. 118, two copies', in her hand. The librarian, who left at six, remembers her coming in and remembers nothing unusual. The library is forty seconds from room 4 by the back stairs.

Scene 11. The toxicology report arrives faster than usual because the doctor asked for it: the glass held digitalis, roughly five times the dose in Askew's own bottle, dissolved in water. His own tablets are a different formulation, slow-release; the glass held the plain kind, the sort any pharmacy sells by prescription. Askew's heart would have stopped within the hour. The coffee was only coffee.

Scene 12. Dmitri Sorel's walk by the canal has a witness after all: a boathouse attendant who sold him a cigarette at ten to six and talked with him about the cold for a quarter of an hour. Sorel is relieved and then, being Sorel, offended that he was suspected. Halloran notes that this clears Sorel for the time of death but not for the glass, which could have been poured earlier.

Scene 13. Agnes Holm's desk drawer, examined more carefully, has fresh scratches around the lock, the kind a bent hairpin leaves. Agnes is adamant that she opened it last on Monday. The master key is in its place. Halloran asks who, in the last month, has sat at Agnes's desk; she says nobody, then remembers that Ruth Kessler used her telephone on Tuesday while Agnes was at the printer's, 'for five minutes, no more'.

Scene 14. Felix Brand, recovered a little, tells Halloran something he had not mentioned: his teacher had changed his will in October, leaving the Bechstein grand and a sum of money to the conservatory's scholarship fund 'in Felix's name', and had told Felix so. Felix is embarrassed to say it. Vera Askew, asked separately, says she knew nothing of any new will.

Scene 15. Vera Askew's lover turns out to be a cellist from the city orchestra who was playing in a concert across town that evening, in front of six hundred people. Vera's own afternoon is accounted for by a hairdresser until five and the hall from half past, where the usher remembers her. She inherits the apartment and little else; the new will leaves the rest to the scholarship fund.

Scene 16. Ruth Kessler's pharmacy. Halloran, working through the suspects' prescriptions, finds that Ruth's mother, with whom she lives, has a heart condition and is prescribed plain digitalis, and that Ruth collects it for her monthly. The last collection was two weeks ago. Ruth, told this, says of course, half the old people in the city take it, and asks whether the inspector has checked Vera's medicine cabinet too. Halloran has: nothing.

Scene 17. The caretaker, going through the building the morning after, finds a brass key on the floor of the second-floor library, under the sign-out desk. It is the key to practice room 4; or rather, it is a key to room 4, because the original is still in the lock of the broken door, in an evidence bag. Agnes Holm says there has never been a duplicate. The new key is bright, recently cut.

Scene 18. The locksmith on Nørregade remembers the key: cut ten days ago from an impression in wax, brought in by a woman who said it was for her mother's flat and paid cash. He describes her as 'ordinary, forties, musician's hands, I noticed because she drummed on the counter'. Agnes Holm is fifty-eight and does not play. Vera Askew is forty-four and does not play. Ruth Kessler is forty-one and plays six hours a day.

Scene 19. Halloran puts it together without yet saying it. The coffee was Felix's and harmless. The water was already on the piano when Askew came in at four, poured, as the caretaker now recalls, by 'one of the women' who was setting out glasses for the teachers that afternoon. Ruth had the duplicate key cut from the wax impression she took while using Agnes's telephone, let herself into room 4 while Pirk was tuning alone for ten minutes, locked it again from outside with the sticking key's trick, and went to the library to sign the book.

Scene 20. Ruth Kessler admits it when shown the key and the locksmith's statement. Askew had promised her, two years running, the accompanist's post on the faculty, with the pension that went with it, and had given it that autumn to a younger man from Leipzig while telling her she was 'the soul of the department'. She had decided in October, had the key cut in November, and used her mother's prescription. She is taken from the conservatory by the side door, during the recital that was held after all.
